summary: Provides a mechanism for a host that uses 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery to get reachability services across a network that uses RPL for routing, without itself taking part in RPL. It updates RFC 6550, RFC 6775, and RFC 8505.

eli5.summary: A simple device that does not know the routing system can still be reached, because the network registers it on its behalf.

subtitle: How a simple device that knows nothing about RPL still gets routed to, because its router speaks RPL for it.

tldr.problem: In a low-power wireless network that routes with RPL, some hosts are too small, too constrained or too risky to run RPL themselves, yet other nodes still need to reach them.
tldr.mechanism: The host registers its address with its router using 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery. The router then advertises a host route for it into RPL, and the RPL root proxies the keep-alive checks with the 6LoWPAN border router.
tldr.outcome: RPL-unaware leaves get reachability without joining RPL, and they cannot mount RPL insider attacks. The RFC updates RFC 6550, RFC 6775 and RFC 8505 and has itself been updated since.

facts.label: RPL Option type in Hop-by-Hop header

today: RFC 9010 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6550, RFC 6775 and RFC 8505. It has itself been updated by RFC 9685 and RFC 9926, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: Why Leaves Need Help
sections.content:
Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs) are built around saving energy, so memory, radio time and code space are all scarce. RPL, defined in RFC 6550, is the IPv6 routing protocol for these networks. It builds a DODAG (a Destination-Oriented Directed Acyclic Graph) that is optimized for reaching a root, rather than for shortest paths between any two nodes.

A host that is reachable over the RPL network but does not forward traffic for others is called a leaf. An RPL-Aware Leaf (RAL) takes part in RPL. An RPL-Unaware Leaf (RUL) does not, and relies on its router to inject routes to its addresses into RPL. The RFC gives three reasons a node might not take part: it is very energy constrained, it is code-space constrained, or it would be unsafe to let it inject routes.

The idea is that the RUL is a 6LoWPAN Node (6LN) and its router is a 6LoWPAN Router (6LR). The RUL uses the 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery (ND) address registration to signal that the router must inject a host route for the registered address. The RFC names energy-constrained sensors such as window smash sensors and kinetically powered light switches as examples, and appliances in a smart grid network as another.
sections.eli5: Imagine a tiny toy that cannot read the map. Its big-sibling router reads the map for it and tells everyone where the toy is.

sections.title: RPL External Routes and 6LoWPAN ND
sections.content:
RPL was first designed for stub networks where the only border router is the DODAG root and every node is RPL aware. RFC 6550 was also prepared for external targets, flagged with the External ('E') flag in the Transit Information Option (TIO), which reach destinations outside the RPL domain. A RUL is treated as a special case: an external target that is also a host directly connected to the RPL domain.

A 6LR acting as a border router advertises external routes with Non-Storing mode DAO messages sent straight to the root, even when the DODAG runs in Storing mode. Packets to the RUL go via the root, which tunnels them to the 6LR with IPv6-in-IPv6 encapsulation. Intermediate routers see ordinary traffic, so only the root and the 6LRs that serve RULs need to be upgraded.

On the host side, RFC 6775 and RFC 8505 define the registration. The RUL sends a Neighbor Solicitation carrying an Extended Address Registration Option (EARO). The R flag asks the 6LR to ensure reachability, and the T flag says a Transaction ID (TID) is present. The 6LR checks for duplicate addresses with the 6LoWPAN Border Router (6LBR) using an EDAR/EDAC exchange (Extended Duplicate Address Request and Confirmation). The 6LBR is the source of truth for uniqueness and ownership.

Without this RFC, every address would need two keep-alive messages crossing the whole network: a DAO to the root and an EDAR to the 6LBR. The RFC removes the second one.
sections.eli5: The helper router passes messages to the toy's address book keeper and to the map-maker. This RFC makes it so the helper only has to check in with one of them.

sections.title: What the RPL-Unaware Leaf Must Do
sections.content:
The RUL needs only a small, RPL-independent feature set. It must implement RFC 8505 and set both the R and T flags to 1 in its EARO. It should request routing services only from a router whose Router Advertisements carry a 6CIO (6LoWPAN Capability Indication Option) with the L, P and E flags all set to 1. It is suggested that it also implement RFC 8928 to protect ownership of its addresses.

A RUL that can reach several 6LRs should prefer those that provide routing services and register with every one it wants routes from. Those registrations should happen in a rapid sequence with the same EARO, because gaps invalidate some routes until the registration reaches them. If the R flag is not echoed back in the Neighbor Advertisement, the RUL MUST assume route injection failed and SHOULD try another 6LR.

Because the RUL is a plain IPv6 host per RFC 8504, it is not required to decapsulate IPv6-in-IPv6, since the tunnel ends at the parent 6LR. It skips an unrecognized RPL Option (type 0x23) in a Hop-by-Hop header. It ignores a Routing Header of type 3 when Segments Left is zero. When Segments Left is non-zero, it discards the packet and sends an ICMP Parameter Problem with Code 0.
sections.eli5: The toy only has to say "please look after me" in a polite, standard way, and speak up if nobody answers. It does not need to understand the fancy mail wrapping.

sections.title: Changes to RPL Messages
sections.content:
The RFC makes three changes to RPL itself. First, it updates the RPL Target option so that a DAO can carry the Registration Ownership Verifier (ROVR), a field of 64 to 256 bits that proves who owns a registration. New flags are 'F' (the Target Prefix holds the complete 128-bit address of the advertising node) and 'X' (the root is asked to perform a proxy EDAR/EDAC exchange). A ROVR Size field of 1, 2, 3 or 4 means 64, 128, 192 or 256 bits, and 0 means a legacy Target option. A value above 4 means the size is undetermined, and an implementation SHOULD pass the whole option upward unchanged.

Second, it defines a new 'P' flag, "Root Proxies EDAR/EDAC", in the DODAG Configuration option. The root sets it in its DIOs to say it supports the proxy operation and the updated Target option. Legacy parents copy the option unmodified, so the flag spreads to the whole DODAG. For MOP value 7, an implementation MUST assume the root performs the proxy operation.

Third, it embeds 6LoWPAN ND status codes in the RPL Status used in DAO-ACK and DCO messages. The RPL Status becomes a one-byte field with a 'U' bit (rejection), an 'A' bit (the value is a 6LoWPAN ND status) and a 6-bit Status Value. To make this fit, the range of ARO/EARO Status values is cut to 0-63. The RFC also extends the Destination Cleanup Object (DCO) from RFC 9009 to Non-Storing mode, so the root can report problems directly to the 6LR.
sections.eli5: The notes passed between routers get a few extra boxes to tick: who really owns this address, whether the root should do the checking, and whether something went wrong.

sections.title: How Unicast Registration Works
sections.content:
On the first registration, the 6LR receives the NS(EARO) and runs the EDAR/EDAC duplicate-address check with the 6LBR itself, because the address must be verified before it is injected. If that fails, the 6LR returns a non-zero status and creates no neighbor cache entry. If it succeeds, the 6LR creates the entry and sends a Non-Storing DAO with the 'K' flag set, asking for a DAO-ACK. When the DAO-ACK arrives, the 6LR answers the RUL with an NA(EARO).

On refreshes, the 6LR must not send its own EDAR when the root's 'P' flag is 1. It sets 'X' to 1 in the DAO's Target option, and the root performs the EDAR/EDAC exchange with the 6LBR on its behalf. The DAO's Path Sequence is taken from the TID, and the Path Lifetime is computed from the Registration Lifetime so that it outlasts the registration and the round trip to the root. If the 'P' flag is 0, the 6LR must handle EDAR/EDAC itself.

The 6LR sets the R flag to 1 in the NA(EARO) if and only if the DAO-ACK's 'U' flag is 0, meaning the route was injected and the proxied exchange succeeded. If the route could not be installed for a reason unrelated to ND, the registration still succeeds but R is 0, so the RUL has a binding and no route. A registration lifetime of 0 becomes a No-Path DAO with a Path Lifetime of 0. An asynchronous problem, such as a negative status from a 6LoWPAN Backbone Router, travels back as a DCO from the root and then as an asynchronous NA(EARO) to the RUL.

If the network uses Address-Protected ND and the status is 5 (Validation Requested), the 6LR MUST challenge the RUL to prove ownership before the address is injected into RPL.
sections.eli5: The first time, the helper checks the address book itself. After that, the helper just tells the root "still here", and the root keeps the address book up to date.

sections.title: Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
Multicast support applies only when the RPL Instance uses MOP value 3 ("Storing Mode of Operation with multicast support"). The RUL acts as an MLD listener (RFC 3810) and the 6LR acts as the MLD querier. The RFC does not change MLD.

When the RUL sends an unsolicited Report, the 6LR sends a DAO with the multicast address as the Target Prefix. The root, if it is not yet a listener for that address, sends its own unsolicited Report toward the 6LBR, which acts as the querier on the root's link. Refreshes are pulled by the 6LR, which sends Multicast Address Specific Queries to its listeners each Query Interval and re-advertises the aggregated list in DAOs. The root lists each multicast address exactly once in its Reports.
sections.eli5: For group messages, the helper asks the toys which groups they want to hear, and tells the root, who tells the outside world.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
With plain RPL every node can inject RPL-based attacks. Keeping RULs on 6LoWPAN ND means they cannot perform RPL insider attacks. The network still depends on its 6LBR and RPL participants, so a trust model is needed, at minimum based on Layer 2 secure joining and link-layer security. It guards against black-holing, against a rogue 6LR or 6LN causing high churn by registering and removing many addresses, and against an impersonated 6LBR using status code 4 ("Removed") to destroy state.

The RFC suggests using RFC 8928 to reduce the attack surface further. A RUL could also send a forged RPL Option to grab a reserved RPL Instance. The 6LR has the final word and its policy may override the RUL's suggested instance. When a Target option has an unknown ROVR size, it is passed on as received, which could be a covert channel, so an implementation SHOULD notify network management when that happens.
sections.eli5: Keeping the toys out of the routing talk means a naughty toy cannot spread false directions. The grown-up routers still need to trust each other.

viz.caption: UPDATED RPL TARGET OPTION, FIXED PART (RFC 9010)

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Target Prefix holds the full 128-bit address of the advertiser.

fields.name: X
fields.desc: Asks the root to proxy the EDAR/EDAC exchange.

fields.name: Flg
fields.desc: Reserved; set to 0 and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: ROVRsz
fields.desc: 1 to 4 means a ROVR of 64, 128, 192 or 256 bits; 0 for a legacy option.

fields.name: Prefix Length
fields.desc: Bits of the advertised prefix; 128 for a host route.

messages.label: NS(EARO)
messages.note: Registers the address with R and T set.

messages.label: DAO (X=0)
messages.note: Injects the host route in Non-Storing mode.
